strengths: A very elegant and novel perspective on visual generative classification: identifying and resolving the fixed-token-order inductive bias of visual autoregressive (AR) models using any-order AR modeling.

Remarkable performance improvement over previous state-of-the-art generative classifiers (GCs), such as diffusion-based classifiers (DiT, SiT) and other AR classifiers (VAR, LlamaGen), on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks.

Excellent efficiency gains: the proposed order-marginalized AR model evaluates likelihoods much faster than diffusion-based classifiers, offering up to a 25× speedup while maintaining superior accuracy.

Comprehensive and well-structured experiments, including detailed ablations on tokenizers, likelihood estimation strategies, the effect of prefix length, and evaluations on real-world distribution shifts (WILDS).

Strong qualitative insights, such as visualizing per-token discriminative log-likelihoods, which effectively demonstrate how marginalizing over multiple token orders captures more comprehensive class-specific attributes.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution relies heavily on existing pre-trained any-order AR models (specifically, RandAR). The classification framework itself is a direct application of order marginalization.

While significantly faster than diffusion-based classifiers, the computational cost of generative classification remains highly demanding compared to standard discriminative models because it requires scaling linearly with the number of classes (i.e., evaluating $p(x|c)$ for all classes $c$).

strengths: Well-motivated and elegant core idea: The authors address a critical limitation of autoregressive generative classifiers (fixed raster order) by leveraging any-order AR models (RandAR) and proposing an order-marginalized likelihood estimation framework.

Excellent performance and efficiency: The proposed method consistently outperforms diffusion-based classifiers (e.g., DiT, SiT) across multiple benchmarks while achieving up to 25x faster inference, which is a major step forward for generative classifiers.

Comprehensive and rigorous experiments: The evaluation is thorough, spanning standard ImageNet classification, out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets (ImageNet-R/S/A/C), and real-world distribution shifts via the WILDS benchmark.

Insightful analysis and visualizations: The paper provides great depth in analyzing the behavior of the model, including per-token discriminative log-likelihood maps (showing how marginalization captures object shapes), token accuracy vs. prefix length, and tokenizer robustness.
weaknesses: Reliance on Any-Order AR Models: The proposed approach is fundamentally tied to any-order AR models like RandAR. Standard and popular visual AR models (e.g., LlamaGen, VAR) cannot be used directly without being retrained from scratch in a random-order fashion. The authors should explicitly highlight this dependency as a limitation.

High Training and Inference Computational Costs: Generative classification remains extremely computationally expensive because likelihood evaluation scales with the number of classes. For ImageNet (1000 classes) and K=20, evaluating one image requires substantial compute. Furthermore, the paper mentions retraining RandAR models from scratch with latent noise augmentation; details regarding the exact GPU hours/resources needed for this training are missing.

Lack of Class-Conditional Baseline Comparisons on Generation Quality: Since the generative models are retrained (e.g., with latent noise augmentation for LlamaGen tokenizer), it is unclear if these modifications affect the original generation capability (e.g., FID score) of the models. It would be helpful to show if the proposed noise augmentation hurts or helps generative quality while improving classification.

strengths: Clear and original insight: The paper successfully identifies that the fixed-token-order constraint in traditional visual autoregressive (AR) models acts as a restrictive inductive bias for generative classification. Addressing this by marginalizing over multiple token orders using an any-order AR model (RandAR) is highly intuitive.

State-of-the-art results: The proposed order-marginalized AR classifier consistently outperforms previous generative classifiers, including diffusion classifiers (DiT, SiT) and prior AR classifiers (VAR, LlamaGen), across in-domain and out-of-distribution (OOD) ImageNet benchmarks.

Significant efficiency gains: By providing explicit likelihoods in fewer forward passes, the proposed method achieves up to 25× faster inference compared to diffusion-based classifiers while achieving superior accuracy.

Thorough analysis and ablation studies: The paper offers insightful analyses on per-token discriminative log-likelihoods, token accuracy in relation to prefix length, the impact of VQ-VAE tokenizers, and robustness under real-world distribution shifts (WILDS).
weaknesses: Clarification needed on class conditioning and attention masking: The text states that class tokens are 'appended' to the end of each permuted sequence (Section 4 and Figure 2). Under standard causal autoregressive masking, tokens cannot attend to subsequent tokens. If the class token is at the end, it is unclear how the likelihood of preceding image tokens is conditioned on it. If the class token is actually prepended, then key-value (KV) caching across different classes is not possible, which would require $M \times K$ full forward passes. Clarification on the exact masking mechanism and KV-cache utilization is necessary.

High absolute computational cost: While the proposed method is much faster than diffusion classifiers, an inference time of ~20-30 seconds per image on an A100 GPU (for $K=20$) is still extremely slow compared to discriminative classifiers, restricting its use to offline or niche robust evaluation scenarios.

Heavy reliance on any-order training: The proposed order-marginalization cannot be applied to other established visual AR architectures (like VAR or LlamaGen) out-of-the-box without retraining them from scratch to support arbitrary sequence permutations.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and overlooked limitation of existing autoregressive (AR) generative classifiers: their reliance on a fixed token order (like raster-scan), which introduces a restrictive inductive bias.

The proposed solution of using any-order AR (AO-AR) models combined with order-marginalized log-likelihood estimation (using Jensen's inequality lower bound) is elegant, theoretically grounded, and highly effective.

The empirical results are exceptionally strong. The proposed method (RandAR-XL) sets a new state-of-the-art for generative classifiers, outperforming diffusion classifiers (DiT, SiT) by a large margin on ImageNet-Val and OOD datasets.

Remarkable efficiency improvement over diffusion classifiers, achieving up to 25× speedup while maintaining superior accuracy. This is a significant step forward in making generative classifiers more practical.

The paper is very well-written, provides intuitive visualizations (e.g., per-token discriminative likelihoods), and includes extensive ablation studies (such as VQ-VAE tokenizers, noise augmentation, comparing AR vs. masked diffusion, and generalization to other architectures like RAR).
weaknesses: While up to 25× faster than diffusion classifiers, the proposed generative classifier is still computationally heavy compared to standard discriminative models due to the need to evaluate likelihoods across all classes $M$ and $K$ random permutations. A discussion or clarification on how KV caching is utilized to optimize this process, and the exact wall-clock overhead compared to a standard ViT, would be beneficial.

The method is heavily reliant on any-order autoregressive models. Because most off-the-shelf visual AR models (e.g., VAR, LlamaGen) are trained with a fixed token order, users cannot apply this method out-of-the-box to existing pre-trained AR models without retraining them under random order permutations from scratch.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly relevant and interesting topic: visual generative classification. It identifies a key limitation of prior AR-based generative classifiers (the fixed token order) and elegantly resolves it by introducing order-marginalized predictions using any-order AR (AO-AR) models.

Significant efficiency improvements over diffusion classifiers: Evaluating likelihood in AR models requires only a single forward pass per token order. Even when marginalizing over K=20 orders, the method is up to 25x faster than DiT-based diffusion classifiers while achieving superior classification accuracy.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: The proposed method is evaluated across a wide range of benchmarks, including ImageNet-Val, multiple out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets (ImageNet-R/S/A/C), non-image-centric datasets (ObjectNet, COCO), and real-world distribution shifts (WILDS). It consistently outperforms existing generative classifiers and achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art self-supervised models like DINOv2.

Thorough analysis and ablation studies: The paper provides insightful analyses on the importance of different prefix lengths, comparison of VQ-VAE tokenizers (LlamaGen vs. MaskGIT), comparison of likelihood estimation strategies (direct expectation vs. lower bound), and the equivalence/differences with masked diffusion.
weaknesses: High computational cost for large class vocabularies: Although the proposed method is much faster than diffusion classifiers, it still requires evaluating the model for each class token (M classes) multiplied by the number of random orders (K). For large-scale classification tasks with thousands of classes, this remains a substantial computational burden. The paper would benefit from discussing potential mitigation strategies (e.g., class-filtering or distillation).

Dependency on any-order AR architectures: The success of the method relies heavily on any-order AR architectures like RandAR or modified RAR, which are less widely pretrained or available compared to standard raster-scan AR models. Training these models from scratch requires significant resources.

Heuristic choice of K: While the paper demonstrates the trade-off between the number of orders K and accuracy, the choice of K is fixed (typically K=20) for all images. An adaptive mechanism that determines when to stop sampling more orders based on confidence could be a valuable addition to further optimize inference efficiency.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and overlooked limitation of autoregressive (AR) generative classifiers: the restrictive inductive bias imposed by a fixed token ordering (e.g., raster-scan). The proposed solution of order-marginalized prediction is simple, intuitive, and highly effective.

Excellent computational efficiency compared to diffusion classifiers. By leveraging the fact that AR models compute the likelihood of a sequence in a single forward pass, the proposed method is up to 25x faster than diffusion classifiers, even when marginalizing over K=20 random token orders.

The empirical results are highly compelling. The proposed method (RandAR) outperforms state-of-the-art diffusion classifiers (DiT, SiT) and AR classifiers (VAR, LlamaGen, A-VARC+) by a significant margin on both in-domain ImageNet-Val and out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks.

The paper presents comprehensive comparisons and analyses, including evaluations against strong self-supervised discriminative models (DINOv2) and validations on real-world subpopulation shifts (WILDS benchmark), multi-object datasets (COCO), and non-image-centric viewpoints (ObjectNet).

The theoretical and qualitative analyses are top-notch. The authors provide mathematical proof of the equivalence between any-order AR and masked diffusion models, and visualize per-token discriminative log-likelihoods to demonstrate how order-marginalization captures global object shapes.
weaknesses: The proposed framework is constrained by the availability of any-order AR models. Standard state-of-the-art AR models (such as LlamaGen or VAR) are typically trained with fixed orderings (raster or scale-wise), meaning they cannot be directly utilized without retraining them with randomized permutations.

While the method is 25x more efficient than diffusion classifiers, it still suffers from the inherent computational complexity of generative classifiers on large-scale datasets, as evaluating p(x|c) scales linearly with the number of candidate classes M.

Algorithmic novelty is somewhat limited as it mainly applies an existing model (RandAR) to generative classification with Monte Carlo averaging, though the systematic study and strong empirical success successfully validate the concept.
